title: Unlicensed and off-label medicines, codeine and aspirin restrictions
blurb: Tell unlicensed from off-label use, explain it honestly to families, and apply the MHRA codeine restrictions and the aspirin rule for under-16s.
question: Oliver, 10, has a fractured wrist and moderate pain despite paracetamol and ibuprofen. A doctor suggests adding codeine. What should the nurse recognise?

teach.h: Most children's medicines were tested on adults
teach.body: Few medicines are studied in children, so many children's prescriptions fall outside a product licence. Formally, an unlicensed medicine has no UK marketing authorisation (for example a 'special' made because no licensed liquid exists), while off-label use means using a licensed medicine outside its licence: a different age, dose, route or indication. Plain English: both are legal and common in paediatrics, but the prescriber takes extra responsibility and the family should be told.
teach.cite: MHRA Drug Safety Update: off-label or unlicensed use of medicines

teach.caption: NICE guidelines flag off-label uses, for example off-label opioids in NG61 and IV levetiracetam in NG217.

items: Be satisfied there is enough evidence or experience to show safety and efficacy.
Take responsibility for prescribing and for overseeing the child's care.
Record the medicine and the reason for choosing it.
Give the child and family enough information to make an informed decision.

teach.body: Proficiency 4.16 expects nurses to understand generic, unlicensed and off-label prescribing. The nurse explains in plain language why the medicine is used, reassures that off-label use is common and evidence based in children, and points out where the leaflet in the box may not match the prescription. Report suspected adverse reactions via the Yellow Card scheme; children are a priority group.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency 4.16; MHRA Yellow Card

teach.caption: Since April 2015 codeine is also not used for cough and cold in under 12s.

head: Rule
Detail
rows: Avoid if breathing may be compromised
Neuromuscular, severe heart or lung disease
Signs of morphine toxicity: stop and seek help
teach.caption: Toxicity signs: drowsiness, pin-point pupils, slow or shallow breathing, confusion, poor appetite, constipation, nausea and vomiting.

teach.body: Codeine works only after the liver enzyme CYP2D6 converts it to morphine. Genetic variation means poor metabolisers get little pain relief, while ultra-rapid metabolisers produce dangerous amounts of morphine, causing respiratory depression. Children with obstructive sleep apnoea after tonsil or adenoid surgery are at particular risk, which led to deaths and the 2013 restriction.

teach.caption: You cannot tell a child's metaboliser type at the bedside, which is why the age and surgery rules matter.

rows.label: Aspirin for a fever or cold

teach.note: Aspirin in under-16s is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious condition after an illness such as flu or chickenpox (NHS).

teach.text: Codeine is not 'safe from 12'. The MHRA rule is OVER 12, for acute moderate pain, when paracetamol or ibuprofen have not worked. And a 15-year-old after tonsillectomy for sleep apnoea must not have it at all: that contraindication runs to 18.

teach.h: Scenario: Ruby, 7, and her epilepsy medicine
teach.body: Ruby is prescribed an antiseizure medicine at a dose outside its licence for her age. Her mother has read the leaflet, which says the medicine is not recommended under 12, and is worried. Nurse Sunita explains that many children's medicines are used off-label because few were tested in children, that the doctor has chosen it on evidence, and offers a child-specific information leaflet. She invites more questions and lets the prescriber know about the concern.

items: Unlicensed = no UK licence; off-label = licensed medicine used outside its licence.
Both are common and legitimate in children; explain them to families.
PGDs cannot be used to supply unlicensed medicines.
Codeine: over 12, acute moderate pain, when paracetamol or ibuprofen fail; maximum 3 days.
No codeine under 18 after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for OSA; no aspirin under 16 unless prescribed.

summary: You can now distinguish unlicensed from off-label medicines and explain them honestly to children and families. You can also apply the MHRA codeine restrictions and the aspirin rule for under-16s to real prescriptions.

A.q: Oliver, 10, has a fractured wrist and moderate pain despite paracetamol and ibuprofen. A doctor suggests adding codeine. What should the nurse recognise?
options: Codeine is suitable as both first-line drugs failed
Codeine should not be used for pain at his age
Codeine is suitable for up to 3 days
Codeine is suitable at half the adult dose
A.why: MHRA (2013): codeine for pain is restricted to children older than 12, for acute moderate pain not relieved by paracetamol or ibuprofen. Oliver is 10.

whyNot.0: Failure of first-line drugs is a condition for use only in children over 12.
whyNot.2: The 3-day limit applies to children over 12 who can receive codeine.
whyNot.3: Reducing the dose does not remove the age restriction.

A.q: A student nurse asks for an example of an unlicensed medicine, as opposed to an off-label one. Which is the best example?
options: An adult tablet given to a 6-year-old
A licensed antibiotic given at a higher dose
A 'special' oral liquid with no licence
A licensed injection given by a different route
A.why: An unlicensed medicine has no UK marketing authorisation, such as a 'special' manufactured because no licensed suitable product exists.

whyNot.0: A licensed product used outside its age range is off-label.
whyNot.1: A licensed product at a different dose is off-label.
whyNot.3: A licensed product by a different route is off-label.

A.q: Isla, 9, has a fever and sore throat. Her father gave her one of his aspirin tablets last night. What should the nurse advise?
options: Aspirin is fine at a child's dose
Aspirin is fine if given with food
Alternate aspirin with ibuprofen
Do not give aspirin under 16 unless prescribed
A.why: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless a doctor prescribes it, because of the link with Reye's syndrome.

whyNot.0: No over-the-counter child's dose of aspirin is recommended for fever.
whyNot.1: Taking it with food does not remove the Reye's syndrome risk.
whyNot.2: Aspirin should not be part of a fever plan in under-16s.

B.q: Ella, 15, had a tonsillectomy this morning for obstructive sleep apnoea. Her pain is not controlled by paracetamol and ibuprofen. The surgeon's junior asks whether codeine can be added. What should the nurse say?
options: Yes, as she is now over 12 years
Yes, at the lowest dose for 3 days
No, it is contraindicated here
No, as she must be 16 or older
B.why: Codeine is contraindicated in all under-18s who have tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea.

whyNot.0: Being over 12 does not override this specific contraindication.
whyNot.1: The 3-day limit applies only where codeine is allowed.
whyNot.3: The contraindication runs to 18, and 16 is not the relevant age.

B.q: Harry, 8, has a cough and cold. His mother asks whether she can give him a codeine-containing cough medicine from the chemist. What is correct?
options: Yes, at the children's dose on the pack
No, codeine is not for cough and cold under 12
Yes, for night-time cough
No, codeine cough medicine is for under 5s
B.why: MHRA (April 2015): codeine must not be used for cough and cold in children under 12.

whyNot.0: Codeine cough products are not for under 12s at any dose.
whyNot.2: Night-time use is not an exception.
whyNot.3: The restriction covers all under-12s, not a product for under 5s.

B.q: Noah, 3, has Kawasaki disease. He is prescribed IV immunoglobulin and aspirin. His mother has read that children should not have aspirin. What is the best response?
options: The team will swap aspirin for ibuprofen
Aspirin is allowed once he is over 2
Aspirin is prescribed in Kawasaki disease
Aspirin is safe if given for under a week
B.why: Aspirin is not given to under-16s unless prescribed; Kawasaki disease is a recognised exception where it is prescribed with IV immunoglobulin.

whyNot.0: Aspirin is a standard part of Kawasaki treatment, not routinely swapped.
whyNot.1: There is no age 2 threshold; the rule is under 16 unless prescribed.
whyNot.3: Duration is not the reason it is allowed; the prescribed indication is.

C.q: Maya, 14, is having codeine for 2 days after a fracture. Her mother says Maya is very sleepy, hard to wake and her breathing seems slow. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give the next dose and recheck in an hour
Stop codeine and seek urgent medical review
Halve the next dose and continue
Offer fluids and let her sleep
C.why: These are signs of morphine toxicity. MHRA advice is to stop codeine and seek medical attention immediately.

whyNot.0: Further doses risk worsening respiratory depression.
whyNot.2: A smaller dose still risks toxicity; codeine should be stopped.
whyNot.3: Leaving her to sleep could miss serious respiratory depression.

C.q: Jake, 13, has muscular dystrophy with weak breathing muscles. He has moderate acute pain after a fall that paracetamol and ibuprofen have not helped. Codeine is suggested. What should the nurse raise?
options: Codeine is not recommended where breathing may be compromised
Codeine is suitable as he is over 12
Codeine is suitable for 5 days in his case
Codeine is preferred to morphine in neuromuscular disease
C.why: MHRA: codeine is not recommended in children whose breathing might be compromised, including those with neuromuscular disorders.

whyNot.1: Age over 12 is necessary but does not override the breathing risk.
whyNot.2: Treatment is limited to 3 days, and his condition is a reason to avoid it.
whyNot.3: There is no such preference; codeine adds risk in neuromuscular disease.

C.q: A community nurse works under a PGD. A child needs an unlicensed oral liquid special. Can the nurse supply it under the PGD?
options: Yes, if the GP agrees by phone
Yes, as specials are made by pharmacists
No, PGDs cannot cover unlicensed medicines
Yes, if the parent signs consent
C.why: MHRA: PGDs cannot be used to supply or administer unlicensed medicines; a prescription is needed.

whyNot.0: Phone agreement does not turn a PGD into a prescription for an unlicensed product.
whyNot.1: Who manufactures the special does not change its unlicensed status.
whyNot.3: Parental consent does not make an unlicensed medicine permissible under a PGD.

reteach.title: Licence, label, limits
reteach.question: How do you explain the licence of a child's medicine to a worried parent?

blocks.body: Unlicensed: no UK licence at all. Off-label: licensed, but used outside the licence. Both are common and evidence based in children. Then three limits to remember: codeine only over 12 for acute moderate pain; no codeine under 18 after tonsil surgery for sleep apnoea; no aspirin under 16 unless prescribed.

items.label: no codeine after T&A for OSA

blocks.text: A leaflet saying 'not for children under 12' does not mean the prescription is wrong. Off-label use is legitimate; explain it and involve the prescriber if the family has concerns.

explain.body: A licensed medicine used outside the terms of its licence: indication, dose, age, route, or contrary to listed warnings. Common in children because age-appropriate formulations are hard to develop.

test.q: Which is an example of off-label use?
options: An imported medicine with no UK licence
A licensed medicine given below its licensed age
A hospital-made special liquid
A medicine in a clinical trial before licensing
test.why: Using a licensed medicine below its licensed age is off-label use.

whyNot.0: An imported product with no UK licence is unlicensed.
whyNot.3: A pre-licensing trial medicine is unlicensed.

explain.body: Give enough information about the medicine, including common or serious side effects, for an informed decision. Explain why the leaflet may not match. Encourage questions and report suspected reactions through Yellow Card.

test.q: A mother is upset that her son's leaflet says the medicine is 'for adults'. What is the nurse's best first response?
options: Withhold the dose until a new drug is found
Tell her the leaflet is out of date
Explain off-label use and invite her questions
Advise her to follow the leaflet instead
test.why: The nurse should explain that off-label use is common and evidence based in children and give her the information she needs, involving the prescriber as needed.

whyNot.0: Withholding without a clinical reason harms the child.
whyNot.1: The leaflet is accurate about the licence; it is not out of date.
whyNot.3: The leaflet describes the licence, not the prescriber's evidence-based plan.

explain.body: Over 12 only, acute moderate pain, after paracetamol or ibuprofen fail. Maximum 3 days. Not under 18 after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for OSA. Not for cough and cold under 12. Not in children whose breathing may be compromised. Not for breastfeeding mothers.

test.q: Sophie, 14, is prescribed codeine after a sprain. What is the maximum duration before review?
options: 3 days
7 days
5 days
14 days
test.why: MHRA: in 12 to 18-year-olds, codeine treatment should be limited to 3 days, then reviewed if pain is not relieved.

explain.body: Do not give aspirin to under-16s unless a doctor prescribes it, because of the link with Reye's syndrome after illnesses such as flu or chickenpox. Kawasaki disease is a prescribed exception.

test.q: Aspirin is avoided in under-16s mainly because of the risk of which condition?
options: Kawasaki disease
Reye's syndrome
Febrile seizures
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
test.why: Aspirin in children and young people under 16 is linked to Reye's syndrome.

whyNot.0: Kawasaki disease is treated with prescribed aspirin, not caused by it.
whyNot.2: Febrile seizures are not the reason for the aspirin rule.
whyNot.3: This is not the reason for the under-16 restriction.
